q: One variety in this valley can be bottled bone dry, off-dry, richly sweet, softly frothing or fully sparkling. Which?
exp: No other white grape covers that range convincingly, and the reason is acidity: enough of it to keep a sweet wine fresh and to make a sparkling base, in the same fruit from the same slope.

q: Clean southern air and a thin ozone layer put New Zealand vineyards under stronger ultraviolet light than European sites the same distance from the equator. What does that intensity do in the vineyard?
opts: It bleaches the skins, which is why black varieties are barely planted
It pushes the skins to build extra colour, tannin and aroma compounds
It drives sugar up so fast that most fruit has to be picked before its flavour arrives
It sterilises the vineyard surface, so fungal disease is effectively unknown there
exp: Ultraviolet light is a stress, and a vine answers it by thickening skins and laying down phenolics and flavour precursors in them. Because the surrounding ocean keeps daytime heat modest at the same time, that build-up happens without the runaway ripeness a sunny warm climate would bring, which is much of why the aromatic whites shout so loudly.

q: A single mountain chain runs almost the whole length of the South Island, and every vineyard on that island lies to the east of it. Which chain?
exp: The Alps stand across the prevailing westerlies and wring them dry, so the west coast is one of the wettest inhabited places on earth while Marlborough and Central Otago are among the driest corners of the country. The Richmond Range is a local barrier between Nelson and Marlborough, and the Tararuas belong to the North Island.

q: Blenheim lies about as far from the equator as Rome, yet its Sauvignon Blanc arrives with an acidity no Roman grower could hope for. What accounts for the mismatch?
opts: Cold ocean surrounds the country, so sea temperature rather than latitude sets the season
The vineyards sit above a thousand metres, and the coolness is altitude rather than anything else
Harvest dates are fixed by law early enough to protect acidity
The vines are grown under shade cloth to slow the ripening down
exp: Rome sits at roughly forty-two degrees north and Blenheim at roughly forty-one degrees south, and they have almost nothing else in common. A narrow island chain in a large cool ocean has mild summers, cool nights and a small seasonal swing, so latitude on its own predicts nothing about a maritime climate.

q: Ringed by mountains and lying further from the sea than any other New Zealand wine district, one region gets hot dry summers, hard frosts and a daily temperature swing no coastal site can match. Which region?
exp: Central Otago is the country's only semi-continental wine climate, and everything about it follows from being inland and enclosed: low rainfall, fierce summer days, cold nights and a real winter. Every other New Zealand region is maritime, with the sea holding its temperature inside a narrow band.

q: Spray programmes, leaf plucking and open canopies take up more of a New Zealand grower's season than irrigation ever does. Which pressure sets that agenda?
opts: Sustained drought, which makes water the limiting factor almost everywhere
Humidity and summer rain, which make fungal disease the standing threat
Spring hail, which strips the shoots in the majority of vintages
Salt-laden wind, which burns the leaves off the vine
exp: A maritime climate delivers rain in summer as well as winter, and warm damp air in a dense canopy is what botrytis and the mildews want. Opening the fruiting zone so it dries after rain is therefore the central vineyard task, and only Central Otago farms in conditions dry enough to change that calculation.

q: Wellington and Blenheim face each other across the water dividing New Zealand's two main islands. What is that stretch of water called?
exp: Cook Strait separates the North Island from the South Island and is crossed constantly by the ferries carrying fruit, wine and tanks between them. Bass Strait divides Australia from Tasmania, Foveaux Strait cuts off Stewart Island in the far south, and Tasman Bay is the water Nelson curls around.

q: Driving the length of the country from the northernmost vineyards to the southernmost, in what order do these four regions arrive?
exp: Northland occupies the far north of the North Island, Gisborne sits on its east coast, Marlborough begins the South Island across Cook Strait, and Central Otago lies deep inland in the south. Nothing commercial is planted south of Central Otago, which makes it the end of the drive.

q: A grape glut in the mid-1980s had the government paying growers to pull vines out, and roughly a quarter of the national vineyard came out of the ground. Which variety lost the most?
exp: Muller-Thurgau was a German crossing planted for volume, and it was the country's most planted variety well into the early 1990s, making cheap off-dry white sold in flagons and casks. The vine pull cleared the ground that Sauvignon Blanc and Chardonnay then took, and New Zealand's identity abroad changed completely within a decade.

q: A producer wants Nelson printed on the front of a wine blended from seventy percent Nelson fruit and thirty percent Marlborough. Why is that label not allowed?
opts: Blending fruit across regional boundaries is prohibited outright in New Zealand
Nelson holds no registered name, so it may never appear on a label at all
A stated place must account for at least eighty-five percent of the wine
Marlborough fruit may only ever be sold under the Marlborough name
exp: One threshold governs place, grape and vintage alike, and seventy percent falls short of it, so this blend may be labelled New Zealand but not Nelson. The registered name settles where the fruit grew and nothing more: it sets no rule on which grape is planted, how heavily it crops or how long the wine spends in oak.

q: Broad, flat and floored with rounded stones dropped by a braided river on its way to the sea, this is where Marlborough's first modern vines went in. Which valley?
exp: The Wairau runs west to east and empties into Cloudy Bay, and its free-draining stony terraces are the classic ground for Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc. The Waihopai is a tributary valley opening into it from the south, and Moutere belongs to Nelson on the other side of the ranges.

q: Higher, drier, windier and wide open to the ocean, this Marlborough valley picks a fortnight after its neighbour and gives Sauvignon Blanc of tomato leaf, green herb and a saline snap. Which valley?
exp: The Awatere lies south over the Wither Hills, climbs a hundred or two metres above the Wairau floor in its upper reaches and sits closer to the cold open Pacific. Cooler and more exposed means later ripening, sharper acidity and far more of the green pyrazine character that the warmer Wairau floor loses.

q: Clay-rich side valleys such as Omaka, Fairhall and Brancott run into the Wairau from the south, and growers plant them to something other than Sauvignon Blanc. Which grape?
exp: Clay holds water where the shingle of the valley floor lets it straight through, and that steadier supply suits Pinot Noir. More Pinot Noir is planted in Marlborough than in any other New Zealand region, split between still red off these southern slopes and base wine for sparkling.

q: Marlborough had been out of the wine business for four decades when a large wine company gambled on land the district had run sheep on, and Sauvignon Blanc went into that ground within a couple of seasons. In which decade?
exp: The first modern planting went in during 1973, Sauvignon Blanc followed in 1975 and the first Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc came off the 1979 vintage. Within twenty years that wine had become the way the rest of the world recognised New Zealand, which is a faster rise than any other region in the country has managed. Marlborough had grown wine long before, at David Herd's Auntsfield from 1873, but that business closed in the 1930s and the land went back to grazing.

q: Under a thin skin of topsoil the Wairau plain runs metres deep in old river shingle, and growers in a rainy maritime climate treat that as a gift. What does the shingle do for them?
opts: It stores winter rain and releases it back through a dry summer
It drains hard and holds little, so vigour is held in check
It shields the roots from phylloxera, so grafting is unnecessary
It supplies potassium the vine could not obtain from any other soil
exp: Growing-season rain plus a deep fertile soil equals vigour, and a vine still growing at veraison shades its own fruit and gives thin green wine. Shingle limits both water and nutrition, so growth stops at the right moment without the grower having to force it.

q: Growers set aside Marlborough's coolest, latest-ripening blocks for a use that wants the fruit off the vine earlier than a still wine would take it. What makes those sites an asset rather than a liability?
opts: They hold high acidity at low sugar, which is what a base wine needs
They attract the botrytis a base wine depends on for texture
They give the deep colour a blanc de noirs is graded on
They ripen fast enough to reach the high alcohol a base wine has to start from
exp: A sparkling base wants flavour at low sugar and very high acidity, which is exactly what a cool Marlborough site hands over without any coaxing. Most of the fruit behind New Zealand's serious bottle-fermented sparkling wine is grown there, whoever puts their name on the label.
